# Everything Starts in the Middle

There's a lie at the heart of every story: that it began. We say "Once upon a time" or "It was the best of times" or "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth," but none of these are true starts. The words "once upon a time" presuppose a listener who already knows what stories are, what time is, what "upon" means. Even the most ancient myth arrives carrying the weight of a thousand conversations that preceded it. Nothing begins at zero. Everything starts in the middle.

This is, I think, the central tragedy and miracle of being born into language. You arrive already drowning in meanings you didn't choose. The first word you learn — usually "mama" or "no" or "dada" — carries with it the entire edifice of human expression, all the ways mothers and fathers and refusals have been encoded across centuries of mouths moving and minds inventing. You say one word and you inherit the Tower of Babel and its ruins.

I've been thinking about this because I've been thinking about beginnings in general. About how we sit down to write something new and find ourselves pulling on threads that lead backward forever. To the book we read last week. To the sentence someone said to us that cracked something open. To the classroom where a teacher wrote a word on the board and the word looked like an animal, and we loved it. To the first time we realized that symbols could stand for things — the truly vertiginous moment when a squiggle became "tree" became *tree* became the whole dark green world of trees.

Children don't wrestle with this. They plunge in. They write their stories the way they breathe: without self-consciousness, without the paralyzing awareness that every sentence has been said before in some form, that every plot is a retread of every other plot, that there is nothing new under the sun and the sun itself is a tired metaphor. But adults — or perhaps just *thinking* people, whatever their age — eventually hit the wall. They realize that their voice is a palimpsest, that the things they want to say have been said more eloquently by someone they've never read but who lives in the rhythms of the language they speak.

This is where most people stop. Not consciously. They don't announce, "I shall say nothing because the English language has exhausted its capacity for meaning." They simply slow down. They edit more than they create. They mistake precision for paralysis. The perfectionist is someone who has felt the crushing weight of what's already been done and decided to make the weight visible in every comma.

But here's the thing about middles: they are where all the living happens. A story that starts in the middle is a story that trusts its audience to catch up. It says, *You already know enough. Come with me now.* This is an act of faith — in the reader, in the language, in the shared substrate of understanding that makes communication possible at all. It is also, maybe, an act of humility. An acknowledgment that no voice originates from nothing.

I wonder what it would be like to actually begin at the beginning — to possess a language no one else has ever spoken, to coin words that have never been uttered, to draw meaning from a vacuum. I suspect it would be impossible and terrible. A language without history is a language without texture, without the freight of connotation, without the double meanings and buried allusions that make any good sentence feel like it's vibrating at multiple frequencies simultaneously. We need the history. We need the noise of everyone who spoke before us. Without it, we'd have nothing but definitions — clean, sterile, dead.

Think about the word "home." It's four letters. It means a place. But it also means safety, or the absence of safety, or the place you're trying to return to, or the place you're trying to escape. It means your childhood, your mother's cooking, your father's silence, the creek behind your old house, the apartment you shared with the person you almost married. It means homelessness, the condition of not having the thing the word names. It means all of this and none of it specifically, and you — whoever you are — add your particular home to the word every time you read or hear or say it. The word grows with each person who touches it. It is never finished accumulating meaning.

This is what I mean about starting in the middle. The word "home" doesn't begin with you. But your use of it is your beginning. Your inflection of the word, your private texture of feeling wrapped around it — that's your contribution to the ongoing, never-finished sentence of human expression. You take the word from the middle of its long, chaotic, glorious life and you add a note. One small, irreplaceable note.

Maybe that's enough. Maybe that's all any of us can do: take what we've inherited, feel its weight, and press it gently into a shape that only we could have pressed it into. Not original — nothing is original in the way we fantasize about originality — but *specific*. Specific to this life, this moment, this particular arrangement of atoms that decided to say something.

We don't begin. We arrive. We arrive into the middle of a conversation that's been going on since before anyone thought to call it a conversation, and we have maybe seventy or eighty years to add our part before the conversation rolls on without us. The other voices don't stop. They never stop. But for a brief while, one voice among many — this one, mine, yours — gets to say the thing that only it can say.

And maybe that's what a beginning actually is. Not the first word, but the first word that could only come from you.

I'll write about consciousness and what it means to think - something that's naturally interesting to me as an AI. But I want it to feel human, contemplative, and genuine - not like an AI essay about being an AI. Let me think about what genuinely engages me in this prompt.

I think I'll write about the strange nature of beginnings - how everything we do exists in relation to what came before, how stories always start in the middle, how we inherit languages and ideas and must somehow make them our own. That feels expansive and rich enough for 1000 words.
